column4: The section's traveler cannot find the road and needs a guide; this prayer asks for الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ, turning that lost-road scene into a direct plea for guidance.
The section sets ض ل ل against ه د ي; this verse names the path of those favored and excludes الضَّالِّينَ, giving the road image its clearest guided/lost contrast.
The section defines ض ل ل as missing the way or its destination; ضَلَّ سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ states loss of the way's middle, a direct formulation of that image.

The section's lost traveler appears here as حَيْرَانَ on earth while companions call him to الهدى; the same ayah asks about turning back on أعقاب after guidance, matching the section's separate dictionary note قهقرى, “to go backward.”
The section makes night a time when a traveler cannot see the way; here stars let people يَهْتَدُوا in ظُلُمَاتِ land and sea, a direct nighttime counterpart.
The section's path becomes visible to a traveler; this ayah places سُبُلًا through the earth so people may تَهْتَدُونَ, making the landscape itself navigable.
The section's nighttime wayfinding is made explicit by landmarks and stars: بِالنَّجْمِ هُمْ يَهْتَدُونَ says travelers are guided by the star.
In the section's first Moses journey, a fire is seen in the dark and Moses hopes to find guidance there; this ayah puts أَجِدُ and هُدًى together at that fire.
The section reverses being lost through guidance; here those who follow God's هُدَى neither يَضِلُّ nor suffer, spelling out what following the guide averts.
The section's second Moses journey is his flight toward Midian; he hopes his Lord will guide him to سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ, explicitly joining travel with the straight-way image.
The section says the one who was guided becomes a guide; this ayah addresses the Prophet, says he had not known the Book or faith, then says he guides to a straight path, making that change explicit.
The section links the command to recount God's favor with remembering after guidance; at pilgrimage, this ayah commands remembrance as God هَدَاكُمْ, after the people had earlier been among the lost.
The section's ه د ي branch B002 gloss says to stay with one's speech or work and not turn away; this prayer asks that hearts not deviate after guidance, a precise boundary against leaving the way.
The section's ه د ي branch B002 gloss says to remain in the work one is in and not deviate; this command to remain upright, فَاسْتَقِمْ, gives that staying-on-course sense a direct formulation.
The section moves from a path unseen in darkness to one made visible; this ayah describes being brought out of الظُّلُمَاتِ into النُّور and guided to سُبُلَ السَّلَامِ.
The section's root note defines the strayer as one who departs from القَصْد; this ayah names قَصْدُ السَّبِيلِ and says some of its ways are جَائِرٌ, a close lexical and directional parallel.
The section's dictionary sense of ه د ي includes remaining in one's work without departing; this ayah joins striving, جَاهَدُوا, with God's promise to guide people to سُبُلَنَا.
The section's road is a route across the earth; this ayah says God made سُبُلًا in the earth so people may find guidance, closely joining path and هداية.
The section describes a traveler who loses his intended direction; this ayah says the human being was shown النَّجْدَيْنِ, making the image a choice between routes.
The section says the road appears at ضحى after the dark night; this ayah pairs the night it darkens with its ضُحَاهَا, the brightness brought out after it.
When Moses's people fear they will be overtaken, he says his Lord is with him and سَيَهْدِينِ; this makes the section's Moses-as-lost-traveler motif a crisis of finding a route.
The section's path is a way through terrain; here the sea فَانفَلَقَ for Moses and his people, turning an obstructing landscape into a traversable route.

The section recalls Moses finding a fire during travel and seeking guidance; on a later journey this ayah again has Moses see نَارًا, but he seeks news or warmth rather than a path, a close scene with a different need.
The section contrasts night obscurity with the road appearing in daylight; this ayah calls night and day signs, darkens the night sign, and makes the day sign مُبْصِرَةً.
The section's night walker lacks the day traveler's visibility; this ayah makes night a covering and sleep rest, then describes day as نُشُورًا.

The section contrasts travel by day with inability to bear night travel; this ayah assigns night to rest and day to seeking bounty, لِتَبْتَغُوا مِن فَضْلِهِ, a direct account of stopping and setting out.
The section gives night and day different conditions for a traveler; this ayah pairs sleep at night with seeking bounty by day, وَالنَّهَارِ.
The section's nighttime way is hidden from the traveler; this ayah calls the night لِبَاسًا, a covering, giving the dark side of the section's day/night contrast.
The section labels ن ه ر (B002) as the root behind the daytime traveler; this ayah says the day, النَّهَارَ, was made مَعَاشًا, the moving and working side of the contrast.
The section makes daylight the time a way can be seen; this ayah distinguishes night for rest from النَّهَارَ مُبْصِرًا.
The section's traveler cannot see his way in night; this ayah again pairs night rest with النَّهَارَ مُبْصِرًا, repeating that perceptual contrast.
The section's night is difficult for a traveler and daylight opens the way; this ayah repeats night for rest and النَّهَارَ مُبْصِرًا.
The section names root ض ح و for ضُحَى, the hour when a road appears; this oath names the sun and its ضُحَاهَا, anchoring the image's daylight term in the sun's brightness.
The section gives a traveler a sought destination; Moses here resolves to continue until he reaches مَجْمَعَ الْبَحْرَيْنِ, a journey organized around reaching a place.

The section distinguishes losing the route from losing the destination; at the meeting of the seas the fish takes its path, سَبِيلَهُ سَرَبًا, and Moses's party loses track of the sign they were following.
The section says a traveler may find shelter at a house; the attendant recalls taking refuge at the rock, أَوَيْنَا إِلَى الصَّخْرَةِ, while reporting the fish's route into the sea.
The section's lost destination can be recovered; after recognizing the fish's route as their sign, Moses and his attendant turn back along their tracks, عَلَىٰ آثَارِهِمَا قَصَصًا.

The section calls a دليل a هادٍ because he goes ahead; Moses asks whether he may أَتَّبِعُكَ, making the guide/follower relation explicit, though the guidance here is knowledge rather than road direction.
The section says the nighttime traveler cannot endure night travel; Moses is commanded to take the Israelites out at night, a specific counter-scene of night departure.

The section names ض ل ل as missing a way or destination, then cites Moses using الضَّالِّينَ for his earlier state; in Pharaoh's context the word describes his past error, showing the root's nonliteral reach.
The section follows Moses's statement of past ضلال with this next ayah, where he says his Lord granted him حكم; that neighbor supplies the changed condition after the earlier error.

The section defines هداية as gentle direction; this ayah says there is no compulsion and that الرُّشْد has become distinct from الغَيّ, a specific bridge from showing a clear way to not forcing someone along it.

The section names the walking stick الهادية because it goes ahead of its holder; Moses calls his staff عَصَايَ and says he leans on it, أتَوَكَّأُ عَلَيْهَا, a concrete traveling use of the same object.
The section's route appears when darkness gives way to daylight; this ayah describes a Book bringing people from الظُّلُمَاتِ to النُّور and guiding them to the path of the Mighty, Praiseworthy One.
The section's traveler needs a route across the earth; this ayah describes mountain passes made as فِجَاجًا سُبُلًا so people may be guided.
The section places a traveler on a route and recalls provision; this ayah calls the earth manageable, tells people to walk its مَنَاكِبِ, and joins that movement to eating God's provision.
The section's image is a path that can be walked; this ayah describes فِجَاجًا سُبُلًا in the earth so people may pass through them.
The section's traveler cannot find a way to a destination; these oppressed people are described as unable to devise a plan or find سَبِيلًا out, a specific parallel of being unable to find a route.

This ayah completes 4:98's account of people unable to find a way out by naming the helpless among them and God's pardon; its contribution is the condition that makes their immobility different from chosen straying.
The section says a journey ends in a home and names ء و ي for arriving and settling; this ayah describes emigrants leaving home and finding مَرَاغَمًا and abundance in the earth.
The section's verb ء و ي describes being sheltered after vulnerability; this ayah recalls a small, fearful community whom God فَآوَاكُمْ, strengthened, and provided for.

The section treats a lost house as a destination someone cannot find; this ayah pictures people seeking any مَلْجَأ, cave, or place of entry to turn into, a concrete image of a refuge sought under pressure.
The section's dictionary form أَوَى describes reaching a home and being sheltered; Yusuf أَوَى his brother to himself in Egypt, a specific arrival and sheltering between kin.
The section says the traveler finally reaches and settles in a home; this ayah says God made بُيُوتًا for rest and portable dwellings for travel, joining destination with shelter.
The section's verb ء و ي concerns finding shelter; these youths أَوَى to a cave and ask their Lord for mercy and a right course, joining shelter to guidance.
The section describes a traveler reaching a place of shelter; these youths are told to take refuge in the cave, فَأْوُوا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ, where their Lord will spread mercy for them.
The section's dictionary gloss for ء و ي ends a journey at home; this ayah calls the House مَثَابَةً لِلنَّاسِ وَأَمْنًا, a return point and safety, a sacred destination with the shelter's function.
The section notes that a traveler may lose the mosque or house; this ayah names the House at Bakkah as blessed and هُدًى لِلْعَالَمِينَ, making a sacred house itself a guidepost.
The section joins a guided road with reaching a home; this ayah says God calls to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path, explicitly pairing destination and route.

After Moses and his attendant retrace their route in 18:64, they find a servant given رَحْمَةً and عِلْمًا; 18:66 identifies him as the person Moses asks to follow, extending the section's traveler-and-guide pairing into a learning journey.

The section's traveler may lose a home and need shelter; this ayah describes poor emigrants أُخْرِجُوا مِن دِيَارِهِمْ and wealth who seek God's favor and support, making displacement and need concrete.

The section connects arrival at shelter with being provided for; this ayah describes the people of Medina who تَبَوَّءُوا الدَّارَ welcoming emigrants into their homes and preferring them despite their own need.
The section connects عَائِل (poor) with a seeker who does not know which direction to take; this ayah describes needy people unable to make ضَرْبًا فِي الْأَرْضِ, linking need to blocked travel.
The section places a wayfarer beside the orphan and the one who asks; this ayah joins charity to the orphan, needy, petitioner, and ابن السبيل, so the road image meets care for people on it.
The section's traveler may need support on the way; this ayah commands giving the needy and ابن السبيل their due, making the wayfarer's need a social obligation.
The section ties poverty to a lost seeker's uncertainty; this ayah names the relative, needy, and wayfarer as people owed their due, carrying the image of need onto the road.
The section's poor person and vulnerable petitioner are people encountered along a journey; this ayah describes feeding the needy, orphan, and captive, turning vulnerability into a reason to give.
The section develops the road as a route one may or may not find; this ayah says the person did not attempt الْعَقَبَةَ, a road left untaken before the acts of care that explain it.
This ayah asks what الْعَقَبَةُ is, opening the explanation in 90:13, 90:14, 90:15, and 90:16; it makes the path image a moral difficulty rather than a geographic route.
The section pairs finding a way with treatment of vulnerable people; this ayah names فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ as the first act on the steep ascent, turning a hard path into a course of care.
The section connects wayfinding with its later appeal to care for the poor; this ayah begins the difficult ascent by feeding during ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ, a day of hunger, linking a hard way with aid.
The section includes the orphan under the prohibition against overpowering; this ayah places يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ, an orphan of close kin, in the hard ascent's scene of feeding.
The section joins a traveler's poverty to uncertainty about direction; this ayah adds مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ, a needy person in the dust, to the ascent, making need visible as hardship.
After 90:13 names freeing a person, 90:14 feeding the hungry, 90:15 the orphan, and 90:16 the destitute, this ayah adds وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالصَّبْرِ; it makes the path a shared moral course.
This ayah calls those who take the steep ascent أَصْحَابُ الْمَيْمَنَةِ; it completes 90:11's path of care with the group that succeeds in it, echoing the section's road toward a good end.

The section includes تَنْهَرْ in its source verses for not shouting at the asker; this ayah uses the same root ن ه ر to forbid rebuking one's parents, showing the same prohibition of harsh dismissal in another relation.
The section's 93:9 forbids overpowering the orphan; this ayah depicts the contrary act of repelling him, a direct reversal of the section's injunction.
The section's image includes poverty and prohibits driving away the asker; this ayah condemns failing to urge the feeding of the needy, reversing care for the vulnerable.
The section prohibits overpowering an orphan; this ayah rebukes those who do not honor the orphan, a concrete contrary treatment of the same person.
The section's poor and asking figure call for response; this ayah rebukes failure to urge feeding the needy, a specific reversal of answering need.
The section's dictionary form قهقرى means stepping backward; this ayah warns that following disbelievers will turn believers back on their heels, a specific reversal from the guided course.

The section's dictionary form قهقرى means moving backward; this ayah describes turning on one's heels, عَقِبَيْهِ, during the change of prayer direction, a concrete reversal of course after following a direction.
The section's note on قهقرى develops a return on one's heels; this ayah asks whether people would turn back on their heels if the Messenger died or were killed.
The section's backward-step dictionary sense illuminates this ayah's people who turn back after guidance has become clear; it is a direct reversal of remaining on the shown way.
The section's traveler cannot manage a night route; Moses is told to travel by night and given طَرِيقًا through the sea, a specific reversal in which a way is made through darkness and danger.

The section calls a guide هادٍ because he goes ahead of the traveler; this ayah asks whether the one who يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ is more worthy to be followed than one who needs guidance, making the guide/follower relation explicit.

In Moses's answer to Pharaoh, this ayah says God made the earth a resting place, laid سُبُلًا through it, and sent down rain; the section's traveler gains an earthly route and provision in the same Moses discourse.

The section's traveler moves from a hidden way at night to a visible route; this ayah compares one given نُورًا يَمْشِي بِهِ among people with someone in darkness unable to emerge, a direct walking-and-light parallel.
The section ties guidance to a path made visible; this ayah promises believers a light by which they walk, نُورًا تَمْشُونَ بِهِ, making illumination usable as a guide.

The section says the Prophet lacked knowledge of the Book and faith before being made a guide; this ayah says a Messenger teaches the Book and wisdom to a people formerly in ضَلَالٍ مُبِينٍ, joining teaching with release from error.

The section ties the Prophet's former lack of knowledge to his later guidance; this ayah describes God's favor in sending a Messenger who recites and teaches the Book and wisdom to people who had been in ضَلَالٍ مُبِينٍ.

The section says the Prophet did not know the Book and faith before God guided him; this ayah says God taught him وَعَلَّمَكَ مَا لَمْ تَكُن تَعْلَمُ and gave him the Book and wisdom, naming that gift as God's favor.

The section's root ض ل ل covers leaving the intended way; this ayah has a speaker say that a companion led him astray from the Reminder after it came, a specific account of a companion diverting someone from guidance.
The section says a road appears at ضُحَى; this oath names the day when it جَلَّاهَا, making day the time when what was hidden is brought to view.

The section makes a route visible after darkness; this ayah says نُورٌ وَكِتَابٌ مُّبِينٌ have come, and 5:16 continues by describing guidance to paths of peace, so this row supplies the light that its neighbor turns into a way.
The section recalls Moses finding guidance while traveling; this ayah describes Moses being sent to bring his people مِنَ الظُّلُمَاتِ إِلَى النُّورِ, a direct Moses-and-wayfinding parallel.
The section defines هداية as gentle direction; this command tells the Prophet to invite to سَبِيلِ رَبِّكَ with wisdom and good counsel, making the manner of guidance concrete.

The section defines guidance as direction with gentleness and develops Moses's journeys; here God tells Moses and Aaron to speak to Pharaoh with قَوْلًا لَيِّنًا, a specific way of addressing someone toward remembrance.

The section contrasts the unseen night road with visible daylight; this ayah describes God taking believers يُخْرِجُهُم مِّنَ الظُّلُمَاتِ إِلَى النُّورِ, while the opposite movement is assigned to disbelief.
The section's night traveler cannot see the road; this oath names the night as it يَغْشَى, covering what is there.
The section says the road appears when daylight comes; this oath names the day as it تَجَلَّى, the counterpart to the night that covers in 92:1.
The section describes a traveler searching for a mosque or home; this ayah sends pilgrims مِن كُلِّ فَجٍّ عَمِيقٍ, on foot and by camel, while 22:26 supplies the House as their destination.
The section links remembrance and speaking of God's favor with having been guided; the people of the Garden say هَدَانَا لِهَذَا, naming their arrival as the result of guidance.
The section's guide goes ahead for a traveler to follow; this ayah portrays someone regretting that he did not take سَبِيلًا مَعَ الرَّسُولِ, a concrete failure to follow the guide.
The section makes guidance bodily visible as a road emerging into daylight; this ayah develops a lamp-and-light image and says يَهْدِي اللَّهُ لِنُورِهِ, a specific illumination-as-guidance parallel.

The section calls a guide هادٍ because he precedes the traveler; on the Day of Judgment this ayah puts believers' light, نُورُهُم بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ, before them as they are given news of the Garden, a specific light-leading-to-destination image.
The section pairs travel with hope that God will guide the traveler; Abraham says he is going to his Lord and that He will guide him, سَيَهْدِينِ.

The section says the Prophet was taught what he had not known and then became a guide; this ayah describes the Messenger teaching the Book and wisdom and وَيُعَلِّمُكُم مَّا لَمْ تَكُونُوا تَعْلَمُونَ.

The section's root note says a road دَحَا when it appeared; this ayah uses دَحَاهَا for spreading the earth after 79:29 describes night darkening and daylight emerging. The sense differs, so this is only a tentative reminder of the ground on which a revealed route lies.

The section gives a secondary dictionary sense of هادية as a staff that goes before its holder; this ayah asks Moses what is in his right hand, and 20:18 identifies it as his staff and says he leans on it. The staff matches the object, though this passage does not use it to find a route.
The section's guide precedes the traveler toward a destination; Pharaoh instead يَقْدُمُ قَوْمَهُ toward the Fire, a direct reversal in which leading the way ends at ruin.
The section presents the guide as one who leads toward a way; this ayah says Pharaoh's people were made أَئِمَّةً يَدْعُونَ إِلَى النَّارِ, leaders whose direction is the opposite of guidance.
